data.title: Charts and Graphs
data.summary: This lesson introduces four common types of charts—bar charts, pie charts, histograms, and line graphs—and explains when each is appropriate. Students will learn how to choose the right visual representation for different kinds of data.
objectives: Identify the key differences between bar charts, pie charts, histograms, and line graphs
Select the appropriate chart type for a given data set
Interpret basic information presented in each type of chart
Explain why a particular chart type is suitable for a specific situation
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand basic data types and how to create simple frequency tables.
why: Charts and graphs turn numbers into pictures that are easier to understand. In everyday life, they help us see trends in sales, compare populations, or track test scores at a glance.
Being able to pick the right chart means we can communicate information clearly and avoid misleading others. This skill is useful in school projects, jobs, and when reading news reports.

sections.heading: What is a Chart?
sections.body:
A chart is simply a picture that shows numbers or categories in a way that our eyes can read quickly.  
Instead of looking at a long list of values such as  

```
Monday: 12, Tuesday: 15, Wednesday: 9, Thursday: 20, Friday: 17
```  

we draw a chart that turns each number into a shape—usually a bar, slice, or point—so we can see patterns at a glance.

Why does turning numbers into pictures help?  
Our brain processes visual information much faster than raw text. When we see a tall bar next to a short one, we instantly know which day had the highest count without having to add, compare, or remember each figure. This speed is especially useful when we need to make decisions, spot trends, or explain results to others who may not be comfortable with raw data.

> **Definition:** A chart is a visual representation of data that uses symbols such as bars, lines, or slices to display quantitative or categorical information.

Think of a chart like a map of a city. A map does not list every street name and house number; instead, it draws roads, parks, and landmarks so you can understand the layout quickly. Similarly, a chart “maps” numbers onto visual elements, letting you navigate the data landscape without getting lost in details.

### How a chart works

1. **Collect the data** – Gather the numbers or categories you want to show.  
2. **Choose a visual symbol** – Decide whether a bar, slice, point, or another shape will best represent each piece of information.  
3. **Scale the symbols** – Convert each number into a size that can be drawn. For example, if the largest value is $40$, you might let each unit correspond to $1$ cm, so a value of $20$ becomes a $20$ cm bar.  
4. **Place the symbols** – Arrange the shapes in a logical order (often left‑to‑right or top‑to‑bottom) so the viewer can compare them easily.  

The scaling step often uses a simple proportion:

$$
\text{Length of bar} = \frac{\text{Value}}{\text{Maximum value}} \times \text{Maximum length}
$$

If the maximum length on your paper is $10$ cm and the maximum value is $40$, a value of $20$ would be drawn as  

$$
\frac{20}{40} \times 10\text{ cm} = 5\text{ cm}.
$$

### Everyday comparison

Imagine you are comparing how many apples each friend ate in a week. You could write the numbers down, but a quick sketch of bars—one for each friend—lets everyone see at once who ate the most. This is the same idea that supermarkets use on “best‑seller” shelves: the product with the biggest sales bar is placed at eye level, because the visual cue tells shoppers which item is most popular.

> **In daily life:** Bar charts on a weather app show daily temperatures; the taller the bar, the hotter the day, letting you plan your clothing without reading each number.

### When a chart is not enough

A chart is powerful, but it only works if the data are appropriate for visual display. Very small differences (e.g., $101$ vs. $102$) may be hard to see on a chart unless you use a very precise scale. Also, if you try to cram too many categories into one chart, the picture can become cluttered and lose its clarity.

> **Remember:** The purpose of a chart is to make data easier to understand, not to hide important details. Choose a simple design that highlights the main message.

In summary, a chart turns raw numbers into a visual story. By mapping values to lengths, areas, or angles, it leverages our natural ability to see patterns, compare sizes, and draw conclusions quickly. This visual shortcut is the foundation for all the specific chart types you will learn later—bar charts, pie charts, histograms, and more.

sections.heading: Bar Charts
sections.body:
Bar charts are a simple way to compare different groups or categories.  
Imagine you have several boxes, each representing a category, and the height (or length) of the box shows how much of something that category has. The boxes all have the same width, so the only thing that changes from one box to the next is how tall (or long) it is. This visual trick lets you see at a glance which category is larger, smaller, or about the same as the others.

> **Definition:** A **bar chart** displays categorical data with rectangular bars whose lengths are proportional to the values they represent. All bars have the same width; only their lengths vary.

### How a bar chart is built  

1. **Choose the categories** – These are the items you want to compare, such as “apples,” “bananas,” and “oranges.”  
2. **Count or measure each category** – For each fruit, you might count how many were sold in a week: apples = 120, bananas = 85, oranges = 95.  
3. **Draw an axis for the categories** – This is usually the horizontal (x‑axis) line at the bottom of the chart. Write each category name along this line, spaced evenly.  
4. **Draw an axis for the values** – This is the vertical (y‑axis) line on the left side. Mark numbers that cover the range of your data, for example from 0 to 130 in steps of 20.  
5. **Create a bar for each category** – Starting at the baseline (value = 0), draw a rectangle that rises up to the number that matches the category’s count. The rectangle’s width is the same for every category; only its height changes.

If you prefer the bars to run left‑to‑right instead of up‑and‑down, you simply swap the roles of the axes: the categories go on the vertical axis and the values on the horizontal axis. This is called a **horizontal bar chart**. The same rule—equal width, varying length—still applies; only the orientation changes.

> **Note:** Vertical bar charts are useful when you have many categories and want to read values quickly from a common baseline. Horizontal bar charts work better when category names are long, because the text can be read left‑to‑right without crowding.

### Why bar charts are useful  

- **Easy comparison** – Human eyes are good at judging length. When you see three bars of heights 120, 85, and 95, you instantly know the first is the biggest.  
- **Clear categories** – Each bar stands for a distinct group, so there is no ambiguity about what is being compared.  
- **Simple to make** – You only need a ruler (or a computer) and the numbers you already have.

### Everyday comparison  

Think of a row of shelves in a grocery store. Each shelf holds a different type of cereal, and the height of the stack of boxes on each shelf shows how many boxes are in stock. If you walk down the aisle, you can quickly tell which cereal is most abundant just by looking at the tallest stack. That visual is exactly what a bar chart does, but on paper or a screen instead of a physical shelf.

### Choosing vertical or horizontal  

- Use **vertical bars** when the category names are short (e.g., single words) and you have enough horizontal space.  
- Use **horizontal bars** when the names are long (e.g., “Number of students who prefer online learning”) or when you have many categories that would make the chart too wide.

> **In daily life:** When a news website shows “Top 5 countries by population” with bars that go up, that’s a vertical bar chart. When a school report lists “Hours spent on each subject” with bars that stretch to the right, that’s a horizontal bar chart.

### Common pitfalls  

- **Unequal bar widths** – Changing the width of a bar to make it look nicer can mislead the viewer, because the visual emphasis shifts from length (the true data) to area.  
- **Skipping the zero baseline** – Starting the y‑axis at a number higher than zero can exaggerate small differences. Always begin at zero unless you explicitly state otherwise.

> **Remember:** In a bar chart, only the length of the bar encodes the data; the width should stay constant, and the axis should start at zero for an honest comparison.

sections.heading: Pie Charts
sections.body:
A pie chart is a picture of a circle that is cut into “slices”.  
Each slice shows how big one part is compared with the whole circle.  
If you add up the sizes of all the slices you always get the whole circle, which
represents **100 %** of the data you are looking at.

> **Definition:** A *pie chart* displays parts of a whole as sectors of a circle, where the angle of each sector is proportional to the quantity it represents.

Why does this work?  
Imagine you have a pizza that is already cut into eight equal pieces.  
If you eat three pieces, you have eaten $\frac{3}{8}$ of the pizza.  
To show this on a picture, you would shade three of the eight slices.  
The shaded area is exactly the same fraction of the circle as the amount you ate.
A pie chart does the same thing, but instead of pizza pieces it uses data values.

### From numbers to angles

Suppose we have the following data about how a class of 30 students spends their free time after school:

| Activity | Students |
|----------|----------|
| Sports   | 12       |
| Reading  | 9        |
| Video games | 6    |
| Arts     | 3        |

First we turn the numbers into **percentages** (parts of 100 %).  
The total number of students is $30$, so the percentage for each activity is

$$
\text{percentage} = \frac{\text{students in activity}}{30}\times 100\%.
$$

For sports this is $\frac{12}{30}\times100\% = 40\%$.  
Do the same for the other activities:

- Reading: $\frac{9}{30}\times100\% = 30\%$
- Video games: $\frac{6}{30}\times100\% = 20\%$
- Arts: $\frac{3}{30}\times100\% = 10\%$

Now each percentage tells us how big the slice should be.  
A full circle has $360^\circ$, so the angle for a slice is

$$
\text{angle} = \frac{\text{percentage}}{100\%}\times 360^\circ .
$$

For sports the angle is $0.40 \times 360^\circ = 144^\circ$.  
Reading gets $0.30 \times 360^\circ = 108^\circ$, video games $72^\circ$, and arts $36^\circ$.
When you draw these four sectors next to each other, they exactly fill the circle.

> **In daily life:** Pie charts are often used in news reports to show how a budget is divided, or how market share is split among companies. The visual “slice” makes it easy to see which part is biggest.

### When to choose a pie chart

A pie chart is most useful when:

1. **All categories together make a whole** – the percentages must add up to $100\%$.  
2. **You have only a few categories** – too many slices make the picture crowded and hard to read.  
3. **You want to compare relative sizes** – it is easy to spot the largest and smallest slices at a glance.

If the data do not sum to a whole (for example, test scores of different subjects that are independent), a bar chart or histogram would be a better choice.

> **Note:** Always check that the numbers you plot really sum to $100\%$ before drawing the chart. If they do not, the slices will not fill the circle correctly and the visual will be misleading.

### Common pitfalls

A frequent mistake is to draw slices that look the same size even though the underlying numbers are different. This can happen if the angles are measured incorrectly or if the chart is drawn by hand without a protractor. Another problem is using a pie chart when the differences between categories are small; the slices will look almost identical and the chart will not add any insight.

> **Common mistake:** Using a pie chart for data that do not represent parts of a single whole (e.g., comparing the number of apples sold in January with the number of oranges sold in March). The chart will suggest a false “total” that never existed.

### Quick check

Before you finish your pie chart, ask yourself:

- Did I convert every count to a percentage?
- Do the percentages add up to $100\%$ (or very close, allowing for rounding)?
- Are there only a few, clearly distinct categories?
- Have I labeled each slice with its category and percentage?

If the answer is “yes” to all four questions, your pie chart is ready to communicate the story of the data clearly and accurately.

sections.heading: Histograms
sections.body:
A histogram is a special kind of bar‑like chart that helps us see how **continuous** data are spread out.  

> **Definition:** A histogram displays the frequency (or count) of data that fall inside successive, non‑overlapping intervals called *class intervals*.

Imagine you measured the heights of all the students in your school. Heights can be any number between, say, 140 cm and 200 cm, not just whole numbers. To make sense of many measurements, we group them into ranges: 140‑149 cm, 150‑159 cm, 160‑169 cm, and so on. Each range is a class interval.  

For each interval we count how many students fall inside it. Those counts become the heights of the bars in the histogram. The bars are placed **side by side** without gaps (or with only a tiny gap) because the intervals cover the whole scale continuously.

Why do we use a histogram instead of a simple list of numbers?  
- It shows the **shape** of the data at a glance: are most values clustered in the middle, or are they spread out?  
- It lets us spot **peaks** (where many observations occur) and **valleys** (where few occur).  
- It helps us compare different data sets visually.

### Building a histogram step by step  

1. **Collect the data** – Write down every measurement you have.  
2. **Find the range** – Subtract the smallest value from the largest value.  
3. **Choose the number of class intervals** – A common rule is to use about $\sqrt{n}$ intervals, where $n$ is the number of observations, or between 5 and 15 intervals for most school data sets.  
4. **Determine the width of each interval** –  
   $$\text{Interval width} = \frac{\text{Range}}{\text{Number of intervals}}$$  
   Round this width to a convenient number (e.g., 5 cm, 10 kg).  
5. **Set the limits** – Start the first interval at a convenient lower bound (often a round number) and add the width repeatedly to create the next limits.  
6. **Count frequencies** – For each interval, count how many data points lie inside it.  
7. **Draw the bars** – On the horizontal axis (x‑axis) write the class intervals; on the vertical axis (y‑axis) write the frequencies. Draw a rectangle for each interval whose height equals its frequency.

### Example  

Suppose we have the following test scores (out of 100) for 20 students:

$68,\; 73,\; 75,\; 78,\; 81,\; 82,\; 84,\; 85,\; 86,\; 88,\; 90,\; 91,\; 92,\; 94,\; 95,\; 96,\; 97,\; 98,\; 99,\; 100$

1. Range = $100 - 68 = 32$  
2. Choose 8 intervals (about $\sqrt{20}\approx4.5$, we use a bit more for detail).  
3. Interval width = $32/8 = 4$, round to 5 for simplicity.  

Intervals: $65\!-\!69,\;70\!-\!74,\;75\!-\!79,\;80\!-\!84,\;85\!-\!89,\;90\!-\!94,\;95\!-\!99,\;100\!-\!104$

Counting gives frequencies: $1,\;1,\;2,\;3,\;3,\;4,\;4,\;2$

Plotting these frequencies as adjacent bars yields the histogram. You can instantly see that most scores are in the $90\!-\!99$ range.

> **In daily life:** Histograms are used to show the distribution of ages in a city, the sizes of raindrop measurements, or the speeds of cars on a highway.

### Things to watch out for  

> **Common mistake:** Using gaps between bars as if the data were *discrete* (like a bar chart for categories). Gaps suggest that values between intervals are impossible, which is not true for continuous data.

> **Remember:** The total area of all bars equals the total number of observations (if you plot frequency) or the total proportion (if you plot relative frequency). This is why the width of each bar matters; changing the width without adjusting the heights will distort the picture.

### Quick check  

- If you see a tall, narrow bar, many observations fall into a small range.  
- If the bars form a smooth hill, the data are roughly *normally* distributed.  
- If the bars are skewed to the right (long tail on the right), most values are low with a few high outliers.

By following these steps and keeping the above tips in mind, you can turn a long list of numbers into a clear visual story about how the data are distributed.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Chart
sections.body:
When you have data, the first question is *what kind of picture will let you see the story most clearly?*  
Think of data as a collection of objects you want to sort into boxes.  
If the boxes are separate, named things (like “apples”, “bananas”, “cherries”), you need a chart that shows each box individually.  
If the boxes are parts of a whole (like “how much of my pocket money is spent on food, transport, and games”), you need a chart that shows how the pieces add up to 100 %.  
If the boxes are intervals of numbers (like “how many students scored 0‑10, 11‑20, … on a test”), you need a chart that groups the numbers into ranges.  
Finally, if the boxes are points along a line of time (like “temperature each day for a month”), you need a chart that connects the points to show a trend.

### 1. Bar charts for discrete categories  

A **discrete category** is a label that you can count one by one, and there is no natural order between them.  
Examples: types of fruit, favorite sports, names of countries.  

A bar chart draws a separate rectangular bar for each category, with the bar’s height (or length) representing the count or proportion.  
Because each bar stands alone, you can compare any two bars directly.

> **Definition:** A *bar chart* uses separate bars for each distinct category, with bar length proportional to the value for that category.

Why it works: the visual gap between bars reminds you that the categories are unrelated, so you do not assume any hidden order.

### 2. Pie charts for proportional data  

When you want to show how a whole is divided into parts, a pie chart is useful.  
Imagine a pizza cut into slices; each slice’s angle tells you what fraction of the pizza that topping represents.  

A pie chart is best when you have **few** categories (usually fewer than six) and the total of all parts equals 100 %.  
The area of each slice is proportional to the percentage it represents.

> **In daily life:** A family budget pie chart might show 40 % for rent, 25 % for food, 15 % for transport, and 20 % for savings.

Why it works: humans are good at judging relative sizes of angles and areas, so the chart makes the proportion obvious at a glance.

### 3. Histograms for numerical distributions  

A **numerical distribution** is a set of numbers that can be grouped into intervals, called *bins*.  
For example, test scores from 0 to 100 can be grouped into bins of width 10: 0‑9, 10‑19, …, 90‑100.  

A histogram draws a bar for each bin, where the bar’s height shows how many observations fall into that interval.  
Unlike a bar chart, the bars touch each other because the bins are continuous; there is no gap between them.

$$
\text{Frequency of bin } i = \#\{x \mid a_i \le x < a_{i+1}\}
$$

Why it works: the shape of the bars reveals the *distribution*—whether it is symmetric, skewed, or has multiple peaks.

### 4. Line graphs for trends over time  

When data are recorded at regular time intervals, a **line graph** (or *time‑series plot*) connects the points with straight segments.  
The horizontal axis (the *x‑axis*) shows time, and the vertical axis (the *y‑axis*) shows the measured value.

> **Remember:** Use a line graph when the main story is *how* a quantity changes as time passes.

Why it works: the eye follows the line smoothly, making it easy to spot upward or downward trends, cycles, or sudden jumps.

### 5. Quick decision guide  

| Data type | Best chart | Reason |
|----------|------------|--------|
| Separate named groups | Bar chart | Clear comparison, no implied order |
| Parts of a whole (percentages) | Pie chart | Shows proportion of each part |
| Numerical values grouped into intervals | Histogram | Displays shape of distribution |
| Measurements over time | Line graph | Highlights trends and patterns |

> **Note:** If you have many categories (more than about ten), a bar chart can become crowded; consider grouping or using a different visual (e.g., a stacked bar chart) instead.

By matching the *shape* of your data to the *shape* of the chart, you let the picture do the talking. This makes your conclusions easier to understand for anyone who looks at your work.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.body:
When you first start drawing a chart, it can be tempting to add a lot of detail or to copy a style you have seen somewhere else.  
Unfortunately, many of those choices hide the true story the data is trying to tell. Below are the most common pitfalls, explained step‑by‑step so you can see why they matter and how to avoid them.

> **Common mistake:** *Using too many slices in a pie chart*  
A pie chart is meant to show how parts add up to a whole, usually 100 %. If you slice the circle into ten, fifteen, or more pieces, each slice becomes very thin. The eye can no longer tell which slice is larger, and the chart looks crowded. Think of a pizza: if you cut it into two big slices, you can instantly see which friend gets more. Cut it into twenty tiny crumbs, and you lose that quick visual cue. Keep the number of slices small—ideally no more than five or six—so that each segment is easy to compare.

> **Common mistake:** *Mislabeling axes or leaving them unlabeled*  
In a bar chart or histogram the horizontal axis (the *x‑axis*) tells you what each bar represents, while the vertical axis (the *y‑axis*) tells you the size of each bar. If either axis is missing a label, or if the labels are swapped, the reader cannot interpret the numbers correctly. For example, a histogram of test scores should have the score intervals on the $x$‑axis and the number of students on the $y$‑axis. Imagine a road sign that shows “Speed Limit 60” but forgets to say “km/h”; drivers would be confused. Always write a clear, concise label and include the units (e.g., “Number of students”, “Hours per week”).

> **Common mistake:** *Choosing a histogram for categorical data*  
A histogram groups data into intervals of a numeric variable and displays the frequency of each interval. Categorical data, such as “favorite fruit” or “type of transport”, have distinct, non‑numeric categories. Using a histogram for such data forces the software to treat categories as if they were numbers, producing bars that suggest an order that doesn’t exist. It’s like lining up shoes by color and then measuring their lengths— the measurement has no meaning. Instead, use a bar chart where each category gets its own bar, and the height shows the count or proportion.

> **Remember:** *Avoid 3‑D effects and unnecessary decorations*  
Three‑dimensional (3‑D) charts may look fancy, but they distort perception. A 3‑D bar can make a short bar appear longer if it’s placed closer to the viewer, leading to a false impression of the data. This is similar to a magician’s trick: the illusion looks impressive, but it hides the true size of the objects. Stick to flat, two‑dimensional designs; they are easier to read and compare accurately.

> **Note:** *Check that the scale starts at zero when appropriate*  
For bar charts, the $y$‑axis should usually begin at zero. If the axis starts at a higher number, small differences become exaggerated, which can mislead the audience. Imagine a thermometer that only shows temperatures from 90 °F to 100 °F; a change from 92 °F to 94 °F looks huge on that limited scale, even though it’s only a 2 °F rise. Starting at zero keeps the visual proportion honest.

By watching out for these common mistakes—too many pie slices, unlabeled axes, mismatched chart types, 3‑D tricks, and inappropriate scales—you’ll create charts that are clear, truthful, and easy for anyone to understand.

sections.heading: Quick Review Activity
sections.body:
Think of a quick game: you have a list of small data stories on the left, and a list of chart types on the right. Your job is to draw a line (or write the matching letter) that connects each story with the chart that would show it most clearly.

---

**Data set A** – *“How many books each student in the class read last month.”*  
Numbers: 0, 2, 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 12  

**Data set B** – *“The proportion of a pizza that each friend ate at the party.”*  
Slices: Alice 3/8, Ben 1/4, Cara 1/8, Dan 1/4  

**Data set C** – *“The ages of 30 people surveyed about their favorite music genre.”*  
Ages (rounded to the nearest year): 16, 17, 18, 18, 19, 20, 20, 20, 21, 22, 22, 23, 24, 24, 24, 25, 25, 26, 27, 28, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 38  

**Data set D** – *“The number of cars sold by each model in the dealership last week.”*  
Model X: 15, Model Y: 27, Model Z: 9, Model W: 4  

**Data set E** – *“The distribution of test scores for a math quiz (0–100 points).”*  
Scores: 45, 52, 58, 61, 63, 67, 70, 71, 73, 75, 78, 80, 82, 85, 87, 89, 92, 94, 96, 98  

---

**Chart options**

| Letter | Chart type | When it works best |
|--------|------------|--------------------|
| **(i)** | Bar chart | Good for comparing separate categories, like different models or people. |
| **(ii)** | Pie chart | Shows parts of a whole; each slice adds up to 100 %. |
| **(iii)** | Histogram | Groups numerical data into intervals (called *bins*) and shows how many values fall in each bin. |
| **(iv)** | Line chart | Connects points that follow a natural order (time, distance). *Not used in this activity.* |

---

Match each data set (A–E) with the chart type (i–iv) that would display the information most clearly. Write your answer as a list, for example: **A‑i, B‑ii, …**.

> **Note:** A *bar chart* uses separate bars for each category. It is useful when the categories are distinct and not ordered, such as different car models or the number of books read by each student.

> **In daily life:** Think of a *pie chart* like a sliced pizza. Each slice represents a share of the whole pizza, just as each slice in the chart represents a share of the total (e.g., how much of the pizza each friend ate).

> **Remember:** A *histogram* is different from a bar chart because the bars touch each other, showing that the data are continuous numbers grouped into intervals. It is perfect for the test‑score distribution in data set E.

> **Common mistake:** Do not use a pie chart for data that do not add up to a single whole (like the number of books read). The slices would not represent meaningful percentages.

When you have finished, check your matches:

- **A** should pair with a chart that lets you compare individual counts.  
- **B** needs a chart that shows parts of a whole.  
- **C** contains many individual ages; think about whether you need to group them.  
- **D** lists separate categories of cars.  
- **E** is a list of scores that can be grouped into ranges (e.g., 40‑49, 50‑59, …).

If you are unsure, ask yourself: *Am I comparing separate items, showing parts of a total, or displaying how many numbers fall into each range?* The answer points you to the right chart type.

practice.q: A class has 5 students who like basketball, 3 who like soccer, and 2 who like tennis. Draw a bar chart showing these numbers.
practice.a:
1. List the categories on the horizontal axis: Basketball, Soccer, Tennis.
2. On the vertical axis write numbers from 0 to 5.
3. Draw a bar above “Basketball” that reaches 5, a bar above “Soccer” that reaches 3, and a bar above “Tennis” that reaches 2. Label each bar with its height.

practice.q: If a pie chart shows a slice that is one‑quarter of the circle, what percentage does that slice represent?
practice.a: One‑quarter of a circle corresponds to $\frac{1}{4}\times100\% = 25\%$. So the slice represents 25 %.

practice.q: The test scores of 20 students are grouped into bins: $0\!-\!49$ (2 students), $50\!-\!69$ (5 students), $70\!-\!89$ (8 students), $90\!-\!100$ (5 students). Sketch a histogram and state the shape of the distribution.
practice.a:
1. Draw the horizontal axis with the four bins labeled $0\!-\!49$, $50\!-\!69$, $70\!-\!89$, $90\!-\!100$.
2. Draw the vertical axis with numbers up to at least 8.
3. Draw bars that touch each other: heights 2, 5, 8, and 5 respectively.
4. The heights rise to a peak at the $70\!-\!89$ bin and then fall, so the distribution is roughly **bell‑shaped** (symmetrical around the middle bin).

practice.q: A survey of 100 students asked which language they study: 40 study English, 30 study Spanish, 20 study French, and 10 study German. Explain why a bar chart is better than a pie chart for this data.
practice.a: A bar chart is better because there are four categories with fairly different sizes. In a pie chart the slice for German (10 %) would be very small and hard to see, while a bar chart clearly shows each language’s count side by side, making comparison easier.

practice.q: You have the following data on daily minutes spent on homework: 15, 20, 20, 25, 30, 30, 30, 35, 40, 45. a) Create a histogram with bin width 10 minutes (i.e., $0\!-\!9$, $10\!-\!19$, $20\!-\!29$, $30\!-\!39$, $40\!-\!49$). b) Calculate the relative frequency for the bin $30\!-\!39$ and express it as a percentage.
practice.a:
a) Count how many values fall in each bin:
- $0\!-\!9$: 0
- $10\!-\!19$: 1 (15)
- $20\!-\!29$: 3 (20,20,25)
- $30\!-\!39$: 4 (30,30,30,35)
- $40\!-\!49$: 2 (40,45)
Draw bars of those heights, touching each other because it is a histogram.
b) Relative frequency for $30\!-\!39$ = $\frac{4}{10}=0.4$. As a percentage, $0.4 \times 100\% = 40\%$.

practice.q: A company reports the market share of four products: A – 45 %, B – 25 %, C – 20 %, D – 10 %. i) Draw a pie chart (show the angles you would use for each slice). ii) If the company wants to combine products C and D into a single category, what would be the new percentage and angle for that combined slice?
practice.a:
i) Convert percentages to angles using $360^\circ \times \text{percentage}/100$:
- A: $360^\circ \times 0.45 = 162^\circ$
- B: $360^\circ \times 0.25 = 90^\circ$
- C: $360^\circ \times 0.20 = 72^\circ$
- D: $360^\circ \times 0.10 = 36^\circ$
Draw a circle and cut slices with those angles.
ii) Combined C + D = $20\% + 10\% = 30\%$.
Angle = $360^\circ \times 0.30 = 108^\circ$. So the new slice would be $108^\circ$ and represent 30 % of the pie.

lessons.title: Measures of Centre
lessons.focus: Mean, median, mode and choosing the right average

data.title: Measures of Centre
data.summary: This lesson explains the three main measures of centre—mean, median, and mode—and shows how to choose the most appropriate one for a data set. Students will learn to calculate each measure and understand when each is useful.
objectives: Calculate the mean of a data set
Find the median of a data set
Identify the mode(s) of a data set
Compare the three measures and decide which is most appropriate for a given situation
data.prerequisites: Students should already know how to read a simple list of numbers and understand basic addition and division.
why: In everyday life we often need a single number to describe a group of values—like the average score on a test, the typical price of a product, or the most common shoe size in a class. Knowing how to compute and interpret these averages helps us make informed decisions.

Different averages work better for different kinds of data. For example, the mean can be distorted by extreme values, while the median gives a better sense of the middle when data are skewed. Choosing the right measure prevents misinterpretation in fields such as economics, health, and sports.

sections.heading: What is a Measure of Centre?
sections.body:
A **measure of centre** is a single number that tries to capture the “middle” or “typical” value of a whole collection of data. Imagine you have a basket of apples, each weighing a little differently. Instead of listing every weight, you might want one number that tells you roughly how heavy an average apple is. That single number is a measure of centre.

Why do we need such a number?  
When data sets are large, it is hard to see patterns by looking at every individual value. A centre measure gives us a quick snapshot, helping us compare different groups or track changes over time. For example, a teacher might look at the average test score of a class to see how well the class performed overall, rather than reading each student's mark one by one.

> **Definition:** A measure of centre is a single statistic that summarises the central tendency of a data set, providing a representative value around which the other observations are distributed.

To understand this idea, think about a line of people waiting for a bus. If you stand at the exact middle of the line, you are at the same distance from the front and the back. In the same way, a centre measure tries to place us “in the middle” of the data. Different centre measures use different rules to decide where that middle is, but they all share the goal of summarising the whole set with one number.

Consider a simple data set of daily temperatures (in °C) recorded over a week:  

$$\{12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20\}$$  

If we were to describe the week’s weather with a single temperature, we could pick any of the numbers, but some choices would be more informative than others. Picking the smallest value (12°C) would make the week sound colder than it really was, while picking the largest (20°C) would make it sound hotter. A centre measure aims to avoid these extremes and give a balanced description.

Why is a single number useful?  
1. **Comparison:** It lets us quickly compare two data sets. If one class has an average score of 78 and another has 85, we can say the second class performed better on average.  
2. **Summarisation:** It reduces a long list to something easy to remember and communicate.  
3. **Decision‑making:** In business, a company might look at the average sales per day to decide whether a new product is successful.

> **In daily life:** When a weather forecast says “the average high this week will be 22 °C,” it is using a measure of centre to give you a simple idea of what to expect, without listing every day's high temperature.

It is important to remember that a centre measure does **not** tell the whole story. Two very different data sets can have the same average. For instance, the sets $\{10, 20, 30\}$ and $\{15, 15, 15\}$ both have a mean of 20, but the first set is spread out while the second is tightly clustered. That is why we also study measures of spread (like range or standard deviation) later in the course.

> **Remember:** A measure of centre summarises the typical value of a data set, but you should always check how the data are distributed before drawing strong conclusions.

In summary, a measure of centre is a concise way to describe the “middle” of a collection of numbers. It helps us understand, compare, and communicate information efficiently, turning a long list of observations into a single, meaningful figure. This concept forms the foundation for the three most common centre measures—mean, median, and mode—that we will explore in the next sections.

sections.heading: Calculating the Mean
sections.body:
When we talk about the **mean**, we are looking for a single number that represents the “central” value of a list of numbers.  
Think of it as the amount of “stuff” each item would have if we could share everything equally.  
The word *average* is often used for the mean, but remember that there are other kinds of averages (median, mode).  

> **Definition:** The mean (or arithmetic average) of a set of numbers is the sum of all the numbers divided by how many numbers there are.

Why does this work? Adding all the values together gives the total amount of whatever we are measuring. Dividing that total by the count tells us how much each item would have if the total were spread out evenly. This is useful whenever we need a quick summary of data – for example, a teacher wants to know the typical score of a class, or a shop owner wants to know the typical daily sales.

### Step‑by‑step procedure

1. **Add** every number in the data set.  
2. **Count** how many numbers there are.  
3. **Divide** the total from step 1 by the count from step 2.  

Each step is simple, but it is important to do them in order and to keep track of units (points, dollars, etc.).

#### Worked example – Easy

**Example 1 (Easy): Mean of test scores**  
Find the mean of the test scores $78$, $85$, $92$, $88$, and $75$.

1. **Add the scores**  
   $$78 + 85 + 92 + 88 + 75 = 418$$
2. **Count the scores** – there are $5$ scores.  
3. **Divide the total by the count**  
   $$\frac{418}{5} = 83.6$$

**Answer:** The average test score is $83.6$ points.

#### Worked example – Medium

**Example 2 (Medium): Average daily sales**  
A shop sells $4$, $7$, $9$, $12$, and $15$ units of a product each day. What is the average daily sales?

1. **Add the daily sales**  
   $$4 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 15 = 47$$
2. **Count the days** – there are $5$ days.  
3. **Divide the total units by the number of days**  
   $$\frac{47}{5} = 9.4$$

**Answer:** The shop sells on average $9.4$ units per day.

> **In daily life:** If you and three friends share a pizza equally, you add up the total slices (say $12$) and divide by $4$ people, giving each person $3$ slices. That $3$ is the mean number of slices per person.

### Things to watch out for

- **Common mistake:** Forgetting to count the numbers correctly. If you accidentally think there are $4$ numbers instead of $5$, you would compute $\frac{418}{4}=104.5$, which is far from the true mean.
- **Note:** The mean can be a decimal even when all original numbers are whole numbers, because division does not always result in an integer.

### Quick checklist

> **Remember:**  
> 1. Sum all values.  
> 2. Count the values.  
> 3. Divide sum by count.  
> 4. Keep track of units.

Using this straightforward method, you can find the mean of any list of numbers, no matter how large. The mean gives a quick snapshot of the data’s central tendency, which is the foundation for many further statistical ideas.

sections.heading: Finding the Median
sections.body:
When we talk about the **median**, we are looking for the value that sits right in the middle of a list of numbers when they are arranged from smallest to largest.  
Think of the numbers as people standing in a line from the shortest to the tallest. The person standing exactly in the centre of the line is the median. This “middle” position tells us something different from the mean (average) because it is not affected by extremely large or small numbers at the ends of the list.  

> **Definition:** The median is the middle value of an ordered data set; if the set has an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.

Why do we need the median?  
Sometimes a data set contains an outlier – a value that is much larger or smaller than the rest. The mean would shift toward that outlier, giving a misleading picture of a “typical” value. The median, however, ignores the size of the extreme values and simply looks at the centre position, so it often gives a more robust sense of the typical case.

> **In daily life:** If you want to know the typical salary in a company where a few executives earn millions while most employees earn tens of thousands, the median salary tells you the amount that half the workers earn less than and half earn more than.

### Steps to find the median

1. **Arrange the data in order** – list the numbers from the smallest to the largest.  
2. **Count how many numbers there are** – this tells you whether the list has an odd or even length.  
3. **Locate the middle**  
   * If the count is odd, the middle position is \((n+1)/2\).  
   * If the count is even, the two middle positions are \(n/2\) and \(n/2+1\); the median is the average of the values at those positions.  

The formula for the median when the number of observations \(n\) is even is  

$$
\text{Median} = \frac{x_{(n/2)} + x_{(n/2+1)}}{2}
$$  

where \(x_{(k)}\) denotes the \(k\)-th smallest value.

> **Note:** Always sort the data first; using the original unsorted order will give a wrong result.

---

**Example 3 (Easy): Determining the median age**  
The ages are: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13.  

1. **Sort the ages** from smallest to largest.  
   $$\{11,\;12,\;13,\;14,\;15\}$$  
2. **Count the numbers** – there are \(n = 5\) ages, which is odd.  
3. **Find the middle position** using \((n+1)/2 = (5+1)/2 = 3\). The third value in the ordered list is 13.  

**Answer:** The median age is **13 years**.

---

**Example 4 (Medium): Finding the median house price**  
House prices (in thousands): $120k, $150k, $200k, $250k, $300k, $350k.  

1. **Arrange the prices** in ascending order.  
   $$\{120,\;150,\;200,\;250,\;300,\;350\}$$ (all values are in thousands of dollars)  
2. **Count the observations** – there are \(n = 6\) prices, an even number.  
3. **Identify the two middle positions**: \(n/2 = 3\) and \(n/2+1 = 4\). The 3rd and 4th values are 200 and 250.  
4. **Average these two middle values** to obtain the median.  
   $$\text{Median} = \frac{200 + 250}{2} = \frac{450}{2} = 225$$  

**Answer:** The median house price is **$225k**.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to reorder the data before picking the middle value. Always sort first, even if the numbers look “almost” ordered.

> **Remember:**  
> - Odd number of data points → pick the single middle value.  
> - Even number of data points → average the two middle values.

By following these simple steps, you can reliably locate the median for any data set, giving you a clear picture of the central tendency that is resistant to extreme outliers. This makes the median a valuable tool in statistics, economics, health studies, and many everyday decisions.

sections.heading: Identifying the Mode
sections.body:
The **mode** of a data set is the value (or values) that occur most often.  
In other words, it is the number that shows up the greatest number of times when you count each entry.  

Why is this useful?  
Sometimes the average (mean) can be pulled up or down by extreme numbers, but the mode tells us what is *most common* in the collection. This can be especially helpful when the data are categories, like favorite colors or types of fruit, where adding the numbers together does not make sense.

> **Definition:** The mode is the value(s) that appear most frequently in a data set.  

> **In daily life:** If a teacher looks at the scores of a quiz and sees that most students scored 78, then 78 is the mode – it tells the teacher what score was most typical without doing any calculations.

### Step‑by‑step way to find the mode

1. **List the data** – write down every observation you have.  
2. **Count how many times each distinct value appears** – this is called the *frequency* of that value.  
3. **Identify the highest frequency** – the number(s) with this frequency are the mode(s).  
4. If every value occurs the same number of times, the data set is said to have *no mode*.

> **Note:** A data set can have one mode (unimodal), more than one mode (bimodal, multimodal), or no mode at all.

Below we apply these steps to two examples, one easy and one harder, to see how the process works in practice.

---

**Example 5 (Easy): Finding the mode of a short list**  

What is the mode of the numbers $3, 5, 3, 7, 9, 3, 5$?

1. **Write the list and identify distinct values.**  
   The distinct numbers are $3, 5, 7, 9$.

2. **Count the frequency of each distinct value.**  

   $$\begin{aligned}
   \text{Frequency of }3 &= 3 \\
   \text{Frequency of }5 &= 2 \\
   \text{Frequency of }7 &= 1 \\
   \text{Frequency of }9 &= 1
   \end{aligned}$$

3. **Find the highest frequency.**  
   The largest count is $3$, which belongs to the number $3$.

4. **State the mode.**  

**Answer:** The mode is $3$ because it appears three times, more than any other number.

---

**Example 6 (Hard): Determining the mode(s) in a categorical survey**  

In a survey of favorite fruits, $20$ students chose apples, $15$ chose bananas, $20$ chose oranges, and $10$ chose grapes. List all modes.

1. **Record each fruit and its count (frequency).**  

   $$\begin{aligned}
   \text{Apples} &= 20 \\
   \text{Bananas} &= 15 \\
   \text{Oranges} &= 20 \\
   \text{Grapes} &= 10
   \end{aligned}$$

2. **Identify the highest frequency among the fruits.**  
   The greatest count is $20$.

3. **Find every fruit that has this highest frequency.**  
   Both *apples* and *oranges* have a frequency of $20$.

4. **State all modes.**  

**Answer:** The data set is bimodal; the modes are *apples* and *oranges* because each was chosen by $20$ students, the most frequent choice.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the mode can be more than one value. If two or more values share the highest frequency, they are all modes, not just one of them.

> **Remember:** The mode is especially helpful for categorical data where adding numbers is meaningless. It tells you what is most popular or typical in the group.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Average
sections.body:
When we have a set of numbers, we often want a single value that tells us where the “center’’ of the data lies.  
Three common measures are the **mean**, the **median**, and the **mode**.  
Each one summarises the data in a different way, and the best choice depends on the shape of the distribution and on whether any values are far away from the rest (called *outliers*).

> **Definition:** *Outlier* – a data point that is unusually large or small compared with most of the other observations.

> **Note:** The mean uses every value, the median looks only at the middle position, and the mode cares only about the most frequent value.

### 1. How the mean reacts to outliers  

The mean adds all the numbers together and divides by the count:

$$\text{Mean} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n}$$  

Because every observation contributes to the sum, a single very large or very small number can pull the mean toward it. This is useful when we want the *average* of all contributions (e.g., total revenue per customer), but it can be misleading when the data are *skewed*.

*Skewed* means the distribution is stretched more to one side than the other. A right‑skewed set has a long tail of high values; a left‑skewed set has a long tail of low values.

### 2. How the median resists outliers  

To find the median we first arrange the data in order, then pick the middle value (or the average of the two middle values if the count is even). The median depends only on the position of the data, not on their magnitude, so extreme values have little effect.

$$\text{Median} = 
\begin{cases}
x_{\frac{n+1}{2}} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}\\[4pt]
\frac{x_{\frac{n}{2}} + x_{\frac{n}{2}+1}}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even}
\end{cases}$$  

Because it ignores the size of the outliers, the median is often a better summary for *typical* values when the data are skewed.

### 3. How the mode reflects frequency  

The mode is simply the value that occurs most often. It tells us what is *most common*, but it does not consider how far other values are from that common point. If the data have a clear peak, the mode can be informative; if every value is different, the mode may not exist.

### 4. Choosing the right average  

- **Use the mean** when the data are roughly symmetric (the left and right sides look alike) and there are no extreme outliers.  
- **Use the median** when the data are skewed or contain outliers, because it gives a more robust picture of a typical observation.  
- **Use the mode** when you need to know the most frequent category or value, especially for categorical data (e.g., most common shoe size).

Below we apply these ideas to two realistic situations.

---

**Example 7 (Medium): Salaries in a small company**  
The five salaries are $30\,\text{k},\;32\,\text{k},\;35\,\text{k},\;40\,\text{k},\;150\,\text{k}$. Which average gives the most realistic picture of a typical salary?

1. **Arrange the data** (already ordered).  
2. **Calculate the mean**:  
   $$\text{Mean} = \frac{30+32+35+40+150}{5} = \frac{287}{5}=57.4\ \text{k}$$  
3. **Find the median** (the middle value of five numbers):  
   $$\text{Median} = 35\ \text{k}$$  
4. **Identify the mode** – no salary repeats, so there is no mode.

**Answer:** The median ($35\,\text{k}$) is the most realistic picture of a typical salary because the single very high salary ($150\,\text{k}$) pulls the mean upward, while the median ignores that outlier.

---

**Example 8 (Hard): Test scores in a class**  
Scores are $55, 58, 60, 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 98$. Explain why the median is a better indicator of class performance than the mean.

1. **Order the scores** (already ordered).  
2. **Compute the mean**:  
   $$\text{Mean} = \frac{55+58+60+62+65+68+70+72+75+98}{10}
   = \frac{683}{10}=68.3$$  
3. **Find the median** (average of the 5th and 6th values because $n=10$):  
   $$\text{Median} = \frac{65+68}{2}=66.5$$  
4. **Observe the effect of the outlier** – the score $98$ is much higher than the rest and raises the mean from $66.5$ to $68.3$, making the average look better than what most students achieved.

**Answer:** The median ($66.5$) better represents the typical student because it is not inflated by the single high score $98$, whereas the mean ($68.3$) is pulled upward by that outlier.

> **Remember:** When data contain extreme values or are not symmetric, the median usually gives a truer sense of “typical’’ than the mean.

In summary, always look at the shape of your data first. If the distribution is balanced, the mean is convenient and easy to compute. If you spot a long tail or a few unusually large or small numbers, switch to the median. When you need to know the most common category, the mode is the right tool. Choosing the appropriate average helps you describe the data accurately and avoid misleading conclusions.

practice.q: Find the mean of the numbers $4,\;6,\;8,\;10$.
practice.a: Add the numbers: $4+6+8+10 = 28$. Count how many numbers there are: $4$. Divide: $\displaystyle \frac{28}{4}=7$. So the mean is $7$.

practice.q: What is the median of the ordered set $3,\;5,\;9,\;12,\;14$?
practice.a: There are $5$ numbers (odd), so the median is the 3rd value. Counting: $1^{st}=3$, $2^{nd}=5$, $3^{rd}=9$. Hence the median is $9$.

practice.q: A class scored the following marks on a test: $55,\;70,\;70,\;85,\;90,\;90,\;90,\;95$. Find the mode.
practice.a: Count frequencies: $55(1),\;70(2),\;85(1),\;90(3),\;95(1)$. The highest frequency is $3$ for the value $90$. Therefore the mode is $90$.

practice.q: Calculate the median of the data set $12,\;15,\;22,\;27,\;31,\;38$.
practice.a: There are $6$ numbers (even). The two middle positions are $3^{rd}$ and $4^{th}$ values: $22$ and $27$. Median $= \frac{22+27}{2}= \frac{49}{2}=24.5$.

practice.q: The ages (in years) of ten members of a club are: $19, 22, 22, 23, 24, 24, 24, 30, 31, 45$. a) Find the mean age. b) Find the median age. c) State the mode(s).
practice.a:
a) Sum $=19+22+22+23+24+24+24+30+31+45 = 264$.
Mean $= \frac{264}{10}=26.4$ years.
b) Ordered list is already given. With $n=10$ (even), the middle positions are $5^{th}$ and $6^{th}$ values: both are $24$.
Median $= \frac{24+24}{2}=24$ years.
c) Frequencies: $19(1),\;22(2),\;23(1),\;24(3),\;30(1),\;31(1),\;45(1)$.
The highest frequency is $3$ for $24$, so the mode is $24$.

practice.q: A researcher records the number of books read by a group of students in a month: $0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7$. i) Compute the mean. ii) Compute the median. iii) Identify all modes.
practice.a:
i) Sum $=0+1+1+2+2+2+3+4+4+5+5+5+5+6+7 = 52$.
Number of observations $n=15$.
Mean $= \frac{52}{15}\approx 3.47$ books.
ii) With $n=15$ (odd), the median is the $8^{th}$ value. Counting: $1^{st}=0$, $2^{nd}=1$, $3^{rd}=1$, $4^{th}=2$, $5^{th}=2$, $6^{th}=2$, $7^{th}=3$, $8^{th}=4$.
Median $=4$ books.
iii) Frequencies: $0(1),\;1(2),\;2(3),\;3(1),\;4(2),\;5(4),\;6(1),\;7(1)$.
The highest frequency is $4$ for the value $5$.
Thus the mode is $5$ (the data set is unimodal).

data.recap: A measure of centre summarises a data set with a single typical value. The mean adds all values and divides by the count, the median is the middle value when data are ordered, and the mode is the most frequently occurring value. Each measure has strengths: the mean uses every observation, the median resists outliers, and the mode shows the most common category. Choosing the right one depends on the data’s shape and presence of outliers.

key_terms.meaning: A single number that represents the typical or middle value of a data set.
The sum of all observations divided by the number of observations.
The middle value of an ordered data set; if even, the average of the two middle values.
The value or values that occur most frequently in a data set.
An observation that is unusually large or small compared with most of the data.
The overall pattern of data values, such as symmetric, skewed, or uniform.
Another term for a measure of centre, describing where data tend to cluster.
Data that are not symmetric, often having a long tail on one side.

quiz.q: Which measure of centre is most affected by a single extremely large value?
quiz.why: The mean uses every value, so an extreme value pulls the average toward it.

quiz.q: If a data set has the ordered values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, what is the median?
quiz.why: With an odd number of observations, the median is the middle value, which is 7.

quiz.q: In the data set {2,2,4,6,8}, what is the mode?
quiz.why: The value 2 appears more often than any other value.

quiz.q: When should you prefer the median over the mean?
options: When you need the most frequent value
quiz.why: The median is resistant to outliers, unlike the mean.

quiz.q: What does the term 'central tendency' refer to?
quiz.why: Central tendency describes a measure that represents the centre of a data set.

quiz.q: A teacher wants to know the most common quiz score among students. Which measure should she use?
quiz.why: The mode identifies the most frequently occurring score.
